**Answer: Yes.**

**Proof.** Since $f_n \to f$ in $L^1$, we have $\int_0^1 |f_n - f| \to 0$. By the pointwise triangle inequality for real numbers, $|f_n(x)| - |f(x)| \le |f_n(x) - f(x)|$ and $|f(x)| - |f_n(x)| \le |f_n(x) - f(x)|$, so

$$\big||f_n(x)| - |f(x)|\big| \le |f_n(x) - f(x)|$$

for every $x$ (in particular, a.e.). Integrating both sides over $[0,1]$,

$$\int_0^1 \big||f_n| - |f|\big| \le \int_0^1 |f_n - f| \to 0.$$

Hence $|f_n| \to |f|$ in $L^1$. Now, $L^1$-convergence implies convergence of $L^1$-norms (this is the continuity of the norm on the Banach space $L^1$), so

$$\left|\int_0^1 |f_n| - \int_0^1 |f|\right| = \left|\,\|f_n\|_1 - \|f\|_1\right| \le \big\||f_n| - |f|\big\|_1 \le \|f_n - f\|_1 \to 0.$$

Therefore $\int_0^1 |f_n| \to \int_0^1 |f|$.

(Note: the pointwise a.e. hypothesis is not actually needed for this conclusion — $L^1$-convergence alone suffices. The pointwise a.e. convergence is simply consistent with, but redundant given, the $L^1$ convergence by the hypothesis.)

### PROOF COMPLETE
thinking:
The problem asks: if $f_n \to f$ pointwise a.e. and $\int |f_n - f| \to 0$ (i.e., $f_n \to f$ in $L^1$), does $\int |f_n| \to \int |f|$?

Yes. This follows from the reverse triangle inequality: $|\int |f_n| - \int |f|| \le \int ||f_n| - |f|| \le \int |f_n - f| \to 0$.
